text: Hello. My name is Dan Baker, and I'm a data manager working with the
Australian National Research Collections at CSIRO.
My talk today is titled "From Data Entry to Distribution:
Streamlining Biodiversity Workflows with Specify at CSIRO."
I would like to begin by acknowledging the Ngunnawal people as the traditional
owners of the land that I'm recording from today, and pay my respects to
the elders, past and present.
This talk will cover a broad range of methods the data management team has
implemented to support biodiversity data standards that are all connected.
But for the purpose of a linear tool, I'll start with our migration efforts
into Specify and then discuss some of the systems we have in place for data
entry, data exporting, and data editing.
I'll cover how we promote the use of our standards to a large user base
and finish with some comparisons between the collections, highlighting the
similarities and differences in processes and outputs, even with the same
consistent ideologies applied to all the data.
Between mid-2021 to the end of 2025, the
National Research Collections of Australia have migrated five of the
six collections into Specify. This effort was part
of a dedicated project that involved collaboration from the data management
team,
our IT services, project managers,
BAs, testers, and subject matter experts from each
collection that were seconded for at least 50% of their time.
Each collection took 12 to 18 months to migrate with a staggered
go-live approach.
The goal was to standardize the way collection data was managed across NRCA,
increase the system reliability and security, and improve
access and discoverability of the collection's data.
As a bonus, a massive data cleanup process also took place
so that we could map fields into Specify correctly in a way that made sense for the
workflows for the curation staff.
But also so that we could have as many curated picklists as
possible and required fields.
Darwin Core terms were used as a framework, which meant some legacy data had to
be split across separate fields or amalgamated together.
We loaded the data into transformation pipelines, checked for errors and data loss,
noted additional cleanup processes, verified workflows in the
Specify front end, and then performed a rinse and repeat until everything was
verified and signed off by the teams.
We now have over two million registered specimens across the five instances
with over 150 registered users.
Once we had gone live with the collections in Specify, the job then switched to
maintaining those biodiversity data standards for new specimens being registered,
and this can be tackled at various levels.
At the individual field level, we have to make sure the data is relevant and clean.
So well-defined fields in Specify with useful descriptions and wherever
possible, a controlled vocabulary picklist help immensely, which is
something the data management team can control and maintain.
Here we have an example from one of our workbench templates, where we've employed
conditional formatting to highlight fields that have formatting restrictions, as
well as fields that are required or fields that should be
conditionally populated, which is something that the Specify workbench validation
does not cover.
We also have copies of our controlled vocabulary picklists to make sure certain
fields contain relevant data.
The next level up is the collection-specific formatting options that we have worked
with the curation staff on. For this example here, we have the collector name
formats. Each collection has a different way they want the data presented on
specimen labels, but we need to keep certain consistent data standards
across NRCA. Our solution has been to encourage the full use of the
agent table to record as much detail as possible in the separate
first name, last name, initial fields, and then create different
aggregated views that reformat their needs.
We have a VBA script within the Excel template so they can split a list of
collector names into the relevant agent fields.
The last level is the holistic full data approach.
From the data management side, we want the complete specimen metadata picture,
which means putting in checks to make sure things like the country has been
selected for a collecting event, or that there are geo-coordinate values
entered alongside uncertainty and precision fields.
A minimum data set ensures that the information is as useful as possible,
knowing how especially time-consuming it can be to fill in the blanks at a later
date, mostly from finding the physical specimen again.
For this, we have a data check tab in our upload template to catch these more
holistic issues.
All of these additional steps work in conjunction with Specify's excellent
workbench data upload feature so that users are able to
register thousands of new specimens in one go.
The ability to share a data mapping file with the curation teams
alongside our template files guarantees data
consistency on top of the checks and balances that Specify
to make sure things like field formatting and required fields are present.
All of this work to maintain clean and standardized data is important
because Specify is the source of truth for the specimen metadata at
CSIRO, and it is not a closed system where that is only
acceptable to the collection staff.
We use the reporting features in Specify and the statistics pages to
curate high-level summaries to management teams.
We use the interaction tables to process specimens being loaned in and out of the
system and track
exchange events as well. The general NRCA activities
include...
Another fantastic new feature Specify has implemented
is the batch edit option, where users can create a query to pull
back multiple data sets with bulk editing processes.
This has been a great tool for us to help the data cleaning
efforts that didn't
make it in before our go-live deadlines, but also allows
us to update the collections as we go.
We've added common names
to all the tax unknowns in
our
fish
collection and also updated their storage details, which is something that
can need to happen on an annual review of the physical specimens.
To find some of these issues that need the attention of the batch edit tool, we
have created more complex data checks via the SQL-based Power
Query editor in Excel to retrieve live data from the database,
with the subject matter experts generally responsible for checking and actioning.
This further helps adhere to biodiversity standards and helps tackle the fact that
even if you have checks in place to ensure new data is uploaded as cleanly as
possible, there is always legacy data to be reviewed or issues that
arise from adding and editing existing specimen data.
A key component in maintaining these biodiversity data standards in NERRCA is to
spread awareness to everyone using the system on the importance of adhering to
best practices and not have it be a topic that only the data managers care about.
With over 150 users interacting with Specify to varying degrees,
we have to make sure we provide enough training to be able to maintain fair
practices across the board.
Whilst much of the training can be repeated for each collection, there are specific
workflows and data considerations that mean we run special sessions for those
teams. For example, the process of registering and connecting tissue
specimens in the wildlife and fish collections, or the placeholder
registration of a specimen in the insect collection so that labels can be
generated as soon as possible.
Everything we do is recorded and made available, and for each go-live event,
we held daily drop-in sessions for the first few weeks to get users
familiar with Specify and everything it can do.
We also remain available for ongoing support, having a central email address
within CSIRO that goes to the team and setting up Microsoft Teams channels
for users to chat to us and ask questions, but also importantly, to
learn from each other as well. We have an internal landing page where you can
access our various instances, and for each collection, we have created standard
queries and a library of workbench templates and mapping files.
Whilst the majority of users
are guests with read-only access to the data, a key benefit of Specify is
the ability to define multiple roles for different permission sets.
And our standardized roles across all collections allow us to increment the power
that each user has, from data entry for some of the digitization team,
all the way up to full edit and limited delete options for the curation
managers.
However, with all this standardization in place, every collection is different, and
a nice example of this are the labels and reports we are asked to set up
in Specify. Whilst the underlying data structure is relatively
consistent across the five instances, we have a wide range of examples
and varying outputs that we build using standardized templates
to adjust as needed.
In the 28 months since the first two collections went live in Specify, we've had a
tremendous uptake in the usage, with over 50,000 new specimens registered in
that time and over 8,000 new taxa recorded.
The average user has made around 25 actions a day, assuming
CSIRO made them work 365 days a year.
With future work on bulk image processing using the AI OCR
tools mentioned, this number will continue to increase.
So what do we want in the future to help Australia's national collections promote
and maintain biodiversity data standards using Specify?
From our experience, it would be helpful to have conditional pick list handling,
meaning that the options available for users to choose from are dependent on other
data fields.
The recent addition for allowing for multiple table aggregation outputs is great,
but sometimes we need to be able to export two different views of a data table in
one file.
An internal tool that scores your specimens on data completeness would be
helpful to make sure all subcomponents of a specimen are recorded.
And finally, many of the collections want a formal way to create a two-way
connection between preparations belonging to separate collection
objects. For example, in the herbarium, we have sheet preparations
against one specimen that were cultivated from the living preparation of another.
